[ORIGINAL USER REQUEST]
A technology company still earns a third of its profit from a legacy product it stopped actively developing years ago; the replacement product is stronger but lacks a few niche features that the most loyal legacy customers depend on. Maintenance costs and security exposure on the old platform grow every year, and the engineers who understand it are approaching retirement. Some large customers threaten to switch vendors entirely if forced to migrate.

Plan the end-of-life and migration program for the legacy product. Set the sunset timeline and support policy, decide which niche capabilities must be rebuilt versus retired, design migration incentives and tooling for each customer tier, and prepare the retention plan for the customers most likely to defect during the transition.
[END ORIGINAL REQUEST]

[PREVIOUS AGENT OUTPUT]
# Legacy Platform End-of-Life & Migration Program

**Program name:** *Bridge* — a 42-month, gated transition of Platform L (legacy) to Platform N (current).

> **Working assumptions** (replace with your actuals; the structure holds either way): Platform L generates ~35% of profit across ~4,000 customers; the top ~40 accounts represent ~55% of L revenue; sustaining cost is ~$25–30M/yr growing 10–15%; 6–10 engineers hold irreplaceable L knowledge, 4 within 3 years of retirement.

---

## 1. The core strategic call

Three things are true simultaneously and the plan must respect all of them:

1. **You cannot keep L.** Cost curve compounds, the knowledge base is evaporating, and unpatched exposure is an existential (not financial) risk. Time is not neutral — waiting is the expensive option.
2. **You cannot force-march the top accounts.** They are a third of your profit and they have credible alternatives. A migration they experience as coercion converts a support problem into a competitive loss.
3. **"Feature parity" is the wrong goal.** *Job parity* is the goal. You must rebuild the outcomes a handful of loyal customers actually depend on — and you must be ruthless about the long tail of toggles nobody uses.

**Therefore the operating principle:** *fixed dates, negotiable paths.* The sunset calendar is published once and never slips. What *is* flexible — generously so — is the route each customer takes to get there, who pays for it, and what a paid, priced, per-account extension looks like at the tail.

**Second principle — no surprises, no unilateral loss:** you publish the feature commitments *before* you publish the shutoff date, and you accept contractual remedies if you miss them.

---

## 2. Phase 0 — Discovery and instrumentation (Months −6 to 0)

**Do not announce anything until this is done.** An EOL date announced without usage data and a parity commitment is how you lose your top ten accounts in one quarter.

| Workstream | Output | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Usage telemetry / fingerprinting | Per-account, per-feature, per-API usage map for 100% of L installs (on-prem: opt-in agent, log ingest, or paid audit) | Eng + Data |
| Feature census | Every shipped capability, flag, endpoint, report, format, connector — with active-user counts | Product |
| Account segmentation & risk scoring | Tiering + defection risk model (§8) | Sales Ops + CS |
| Cost-of-carry model | True annual L cost incl. security, infra, opportunity cost of engineers, insurance loading | Finance |
| Knowledge asset audit | Which subsystems have exactly one human who understands them | Eng leadership |
| Legal review | Contract-by-contract: perpetual licenses, support commitments, OEM/embedded rights, regulated-industry obligations, notice periods | Legal |
| Competitive intel | Rival migration offers, switching-cost model, likely poaching targets | Product Marketing |

**Critical gate:** you cannot set a credible calendar without knowing *which 40 features are load-bearing for which 200 customers*. Expect the surprise: typically 70–85% of L's feature surface has effectively zero active users, while 3–6 obscure capabilities are individually worth 8-figure relationships.

---

## 3. Sunset timeline and support policy

### 3.1 Support lifecycle states

Publish these as a formal, versioned policy document — this becomes the contractual reference.

| State | What you get | What you don't |
|---|---|---|
| **Full Support** (now → M18) | Bug fixes, security patches, OS/DB/browser compatibility updates, standard SLAs, migration-blocker fixes | New features (frozen at M0) |
| **Maintenance Support** (M18 → M30) | Security patches, Sev-1/Sev-2 bug fixes, existing-platform compatibility only | New compatibility certifications, Sev-3/4 fixes, enhancements |
| **Extended Security Support** — paid uplift (M30 → M42) | Critical/High CVE remediation only, Sev-1 workarounds, best-effort response | Bug fixes, compatibility, standard SLAs |
| **Custom Support Agreement** — bespoke, per-account (M42 → M54 max) | Negotiated scope, capped, priced at 2.5–3× original maintenance, minimum 12-month commitment, minimum contract value | Anything not explicitly enumerated |
| **End of Life** (M42 public / M54 absolute) | Nothing. Hosted instances decommissioned; on-prem software may run at customer's own risk with signed liability acknowledgment | — |

### 3.2 The calendar

| Milestone | Timing | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Confidential briefings, top 40 + OEMs** | M−1 | 3–4 weeks ahead of public, under NDA, exec-to-exec |
| **Public announcement** — full calendar, parity commitments, incentives, tooling roadmap | **M0** | Single coordinated moment: customers, partners, analysts, field, press |
| **End of Sale** — no new L customers | M0 | Immediate |
| **End of Expansion** — no new seats/capacity/modules on L | M12 | Grandfather in-flight projects case-by-case to M18 |
| **Feature freeze** (except adjudicated migration blockers) | M0 | Blocker exception process is the trust mechanism |
| **Parity Wave 1 GA** on Platform N | M9 | Highest-value rebuilt capabilities |
| **Migration tooling GA** (assessment + converter + parallel-run) | M9 | Must precede any pressure campaign |
| **Parity Wave 2 GA** | M15 | Completes committed rebuild scope |
| **Full Support ends → Maintenance Support** | M18 | |
| **Scale migration window** | M12–M30 | ~65% of accounts should cut over here |
| **Standard support ends** | **M30** | Extended Security Support begins, priced at 1.5× (M30–36), 2.0× (M36–42) |
| **Extended support ends; hosted decommission begins** | **M42** | |
| **Absolute EOL / hard stop** | **M54** | Custom Support Agreements only; nothing beyond |

**Runway rationale:** 30 months of standard support gives even a heavily customized enterprise two budget cycles and two change-freeze-free windows. 42 months total is defensible to auditors and regulators. Beyond that, escalating price does the persuading rather than escalating threats.

### 3.3 The security tripwire (state this up front, at M0)

Publish a named exception: *if an unpatchable Critical vulnerability appears in an out-of-support dependency, we will accelerate specific end-dates with 90 days' notice.* Saying this on day one converts a future betrayal into a pre-agreed, jointly understood condition — and it gives your CISO a legitimate lever instead of a fight.

---

## 4. Feature triage: rebuild vs. bridge vs. retire

### 4.1 Decision framework

Score every candidate capability (0–5 each):

- **A. Revenue dependency** — ARR of accounts that would be blocked without it
- **B. Obligation** — regulatory, contractual, or audit requirement (binary multiplier: if yes, rebuild)
- **C. Substitutability** — is there an acceptable workaround, partner product, API, or services path?
- **D. Strategic fit** — does it belong in N's architecture, or would it import legacy debt?
- **E. Rebuild cost** — engineering months, ongoing maintenance drag

| Outcome | Trigger | Commitment level |
|---|---|---|
| **Rebuild native** | High A, or B=yes; fits D | Named in public parity roadmap with a GA quarter and contractual remedy if missed |
| **Bridge** (compat shim, adapter, transpiler, plugin, partner) | High A, poor D — needed, but shouldn't live in the core | Shipped with *its own* sunset date (typically EOL+24m) |
| **Substitute** (services, one-time custom build, config recipe) | Moderate A, high C, low D | Funded by vendor for Tier 1/2; documented recipe for Tier 3 |
| **Retire** | Low A, high C | Named publicly with the replacement path and an appeal window |

### 4.2 Expected shape of the answer

Typically: **~10–15% rebuild, ~15% bridge, ~10% substitute, ~60–65% retire by feature count** — while the rebuild+bridge set covers **85–90% of at-risk revenue**. Say this out loud internally so nobody equates "retiring most of the feature surface" with "abandoning customers."

### 4.3 Common archetypes and the right call

| Archetype | Typical call | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Deep connector to an ancient upstream system (mainframe, legacy ERP, AS/400) | **Rebuild** as a supported connector — or **partner** with an integration specialist | It's the actual lock-in; losing it loses the account |
| Regulatory output fidelity (statutory filings, EDI, print/forms, audit trails, retention) | **Rebuild, byte-exact, with reconciliation proof** | Non-negotiable; failure here is a compliance event, not an inconvenience |
| Arcane scripting/macro/customization engine with thousands of customer-authored scripts | **Bridge**: interpreter or transpiler covering the ~top 90% of constructs; convert the rest as funded services | Rewriting customer IP by hand is where migrations die |
| Legacy v1 API / batch/CLI surface | **Bridge**: compatibility shim with its own published sunset | Buys integration partners and customer IT time |
| Exotic deployment mode (air-gapped, unsupported OS/DB, self-hosted single-tenant) | **Segment decision**: rebuild only if a coherent, priced segment exists (gov/defense/regulated); otherwise a premium Custom Support path | Don't rebuild an unfunded architecture |
| Permission/workflow model quirks, granular admin semantics | **Rebuild the semantics**, not the UI | Cheap relative to the trust it buys; blocks admin sign-off otherwise |
| Long-tail flags, deprecated report variants, sub-1% toggles | **Retire** | This is where you fund the rest |

### 4.4 The Migration Blocker Board — your single most important trust mechanism

- **Any customer, any tier, can file a "Migration Blocker."** Public intake form, no gatekeeping by account size.
- **15-business-day adjudication SLA.** Four verdicts: *Rebuild (with quarter)*, *Bridge*, *Workaround (documented, validated with the customer)*, *Won't fix (with reasoning)*.
- **Public register** — all filings, status, verdicts, dates. Visible to all customers.
- **Cross-functional board**: Product (chair), Eng, CS, Sales, and a rotating customer advisory seat.
- **Reserved capacity:** hold 20–25% of the parity engineering budget unallocated for blockers discovered after M0. They *will* arrive, and refusing them is what breaks the program's credibility.

The register converts "you're abandoning us" into "there is a visible, fair process, and my issue is #47 with a Q3 date." That shift is worth more than any discount.

---

## 5. Migration tooling (the product you must actually build)

Treat this as a funded product with a PM, a roadmap, and its own SLAs. Under-tooling is the single most common cause of EOL programs slipping.

| Component | Purpose | Target |
|---|---|---|
| **Readiness Assessment / "Migration Passport"** | Auto-generated per-account report: features used, blockers, effort estimate, recommended path, custom code inventory | M6 |
| **Config & data converter** | Idempotent, re-runnable, versioned; converts settings, schemas, permissions, workflows; em
[END PREVIOUS OUTPUT]

# Critique: *Bridge* — Legacy EOL & Migration Program

## 1. Disqualifying defect: the deliverable is incomplete

The document stops mid-word in §5 ("converts settings, schemas, permissions, workflows; em—"). Two of the four explicitly requested deliverables are **entirely absent**:

- **Migration incentives and tooling by customer tier.** Tooling is one truncated table; incentives are never discussed at all. There is no discussion of the actual levers (funded professional services, license trade-in credits, multi-year price locks, free parallel-run, co-termination, credits for migration downtime, design-partner status), no **decaying incentive schedule** to pull migrations forward, and no anti-gaming rule — as written, the loudest threateners get the best deal, which teaches every other account to threaten. MFN clauses and audit/fairness exposure from bespoke save offers go unmentioned.
- **The retention plan for likely defectors** — arguably the highest-stakes item in the prompt. Nothing on named at-risk lists, executive sponsor assignment, early-warning signals (champion departure, RFP intel, ticket sentiment, sandbox activity with competitors), competitive-displacement counter-playbooks, rollback/"migration insurance" guarantees, or win-back plans.

There is also a **broken cross-reference**: §8 is cited for the defection-risk model, but the document has five sections. Tier 1/2/3 are referenced in §4.1 but never defined.

## 2. Internal inconsistencies

- **"42-month program" is wrong on its own numbers.** Phase 0 starts at M−6, absolute EOL is M54, and bridge components carry sunsets at EOL+24m. That's a 60–78 month commitment. The headline understates the obligation to the board by a third or more.
- **"Fixed dates, never slip" is contradicted twice.** M42 is "public" EOL but M54 is "absolute," with priced extensions available. Sophisticated procurement will read this immediately: the real date is M54, and the rational play is to budget for the extension rather than migrate. Meanwhile the security tripwire lets dates move *earlier*. So dates move both directions — the principle should be restated honestly as "published dates, capped and priced exceptions, no free extensions."
- **Hosted vs. on-prem is conflated.** §3.1 says hosted instances are decommissioned at End of Life (M42); §3.2 says decommission *begins* at M42 with a hard stop at M54. Which is it? And if hosted is gone at M42, Custom Support Agreements to M54 are only meaningful for on-prem — an unstated and significant asymmetry. More broadly, the policy should differ sharply by deployment model (the vendor bears the security risk and controls the upgrade lever for hosted; neither is true on-prem), and it doesn't.
- **Pricing tables disagree in spirit.** Extended Security Support is "paid uplift" in §3.1 with no price, then 1.5×/2.0× in §3.2, while Custom Support is 2.5–3×. Consolidate into one price ladder.

## 3. Substantive gaps that threaten feasibility

**a) The staffing math doesn't close.** The stated premise is that 4 of 6–10 irreplaceable engineers retire within 3 years (~M36), yet the plan commits to security patching through M42 and bespoke support through M54. Phase 0 includes a "knowledge asset audit" but there is **no legacy sustaining plan**: retention/deferred-comp packages tied to M42, contractor conversion of retirees, mandatory pairing/shadowing and documentation sprints with funded time, hiring a maintenance-only pod, or contracting a third-party maintenance provider. Without this, the support policy is a promise the company cannot keep — which is the exact failure mode that destroys the whole trust architecture.

**b) No dependency end-of-life calendar.** The security exposure is driven mostly by *upstream* EOLs (OS, DB, runtime, crypto libraries, browser). Phase 0 should map every third-party dependency's own EOL date against the M0–M54 window. Compounding this, Maintenance Support (M18–M30) explicitly excludes "new compatibility certifications" — meaning customers still mid-migration cannot patch their own OS/DB without going unsupported. That either forces migration by the back door (breaking principle #2) or manufactures the vulnerability the tripwire then punishes them for.

**c) No financial model or engineering capacity plan.** Nothing on: cost of the parity rebuild, the incentive budget, the professional-services capacity to migrate 4,000 accounts (including partner/SI leverage), the **opportunity cost of diverting Platform N engineers to legacy parity work** (which weakens the product you're asking customers to move to), the profit trough as L maintenance revenue declines faster than N ramps, pricing policy for migrated customers (price-neutral guarantee? uplift?), or the treatment of perpetual license holders. The prompt's central fact is "a third of profit" — a plan that never quantifies the P&L bridge or the investor/guidance narrative is incomplete at the executive level.

**d) Strategic options not considered.** §1 asserts "you cannot keep L" and jumps to sunset. Two credible alternatives are never evaluated: **divesting or licensing L** to a specialist maintenance/roll-up buyer (monetizes the tail, transfers security liability, gives loyal customers a home and preserves the relationship for N later), and **self-funding L via aggressive maintenance repricing** as a baseline comparison. Even if both are rejected, a plan of this seriousness must show the comparison — otherwise the board will ask and the answer won't exist.

**e) Parity dates are committed before the census exists.** Feature census completes at M0; Wave 1 GA is M9 and includes archetypes like byte-exact regulatory output and a macro-language transpiler. Nine months is aggressive for either, and the plan simultaneously offers **"contractual remedy if missed"** with no cap, no definition of remedy, and no legal caveat. Cap it at service credits/support extensions, gate the public GA quarter behind a design-complete checkpoint, and publish "commit" vs. "target" tiers.

## 4. Weaknesses in the strongest section (Migration Blocker Board)

The concept is genuinely good and is the best idea in the document, but as specified it is exploitable:

- "Any customer, any tier, no gatekeeping" + 15-business-day SLA invites volume-flooding and adversarial filing during renewal negotiations. Needs evidence requirements (telemetry proof of use), duplicate merging, a triage tier before adjudication, and a stated capacity limit.

# Legacy Platform End-of-Life & Migration Program

**Program name:** *Bridge* — a 42-month, gated transition of Platform L (legacy) to Platform N (current).

> **Working assumptions** (replace with your actuals; the structure holds either way): Platform L generates ~35% of profit across ~4,000 customers; the top ~40 accounts represent ~55% of L revenue; sustaining cost is ~$25–30M/yr growing 10–15%; 6–10 engineers hold irreplaceable L knowledge, 4 within 3 years of retirement.

---

## 1. The core strategic call

Three things are true simultaneously and the plan must respect all of them:

1. **You cannot keep L.** Cost curve compounds, the knowledge base is evaporating, and unpatched exposure is an existential (not financial) risk. Time is not neutral — waiting is the expensive option.
2. **You cannot force-march the top accounts.** They are a third of your profit and they have credible alternatives. A migration they experience as coercion converts a support problem into a competitive loss.
3. **"Feature parity" is the wrong goal.** *Job parity* is the goal. You must rebuild the outcomes a handful of loyal customers actually depend on — and you must be ruthless about the long tail of toggles nobody uses.

**Therefore the operating principle:** *fixed dates, negotiable paths.* The sunset calendar is published once and never slips. What *is* flexible — generously so — is the route each customer takes to get there, who pays for it, and what a paid, priced, per-account extension looks like at the tail.

**Second principle — no surprises, no unilateral loss:** you publish the feature commitments *before* you publish the shutoff date, and you accept contractual remedies if you miss them.

---

## 2. Phase 0 — Discovery and instrumentation (Months −6 to 0)

**Do not announce anything until this is done.** An EOL date announced without usage data and a parity commitment is how you lose your top ten accounts in one quarter.

| Workstream | Output | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| Usage telemetry / fingerprinting | Per-account, per-feature, per-API usage map for 100% of L installs (on-prem: opt-in agent, log ingest, or paid audit) | Eng + Data |
| Feature census | Every shipped capability, flag, endpoint, report, format, connector — with active-user counts | Product |
| Account segmentation & risk scoring | Tiering + defection risk model (§8) | Sales Ops + CS |
| Cost-of-carry model | True annual L cost incl. security, infra, opportunity cost of engineers, insurance loading | Finance |
| Knowledge asset audit | Which subsystems have exactly one human who understands them | Eng leadership |
| Legal review | Contract-by-contract: perpetual licenses, support commitments, OEM/embedded rights, regulated-industry obligations, notice periods | Legal |
| Competitive intel | Rival migration offers, switching-cost model, likely poaching targets | Product Marketing |

**Critical gate:** you cannot set a credible calendar without knowing *which 40 features are load-bearing for which 200 customers*. Expect the surprise: typically 70–85% of L's feature surface has effectively zero active users, while 3–6 obscure capabilities are individually worth 8-figure relationships.

---

## 3. Sunset timeline and support policy

### 3.1 Support lifecycle states

Publish these as a formal, versioned policy document — this becomes the contractual reference.

| State | What you get | What you don't |
|---|---|---|
| **Full Support** (now → M18) | Bug fixes, security patches, OS/DB/browser compatibility updates, standard SLAs, migration-blocker fixes | New features (frozen at M0) |
| **Maintenance Support** (M18 → M30) | Security patches, Sev-1/Sev-2 bug fixes, existing-platform compatibility only | New compatibility certifications, Sev-3/4 fixes, enhancements |
| **Extended Security Support** — paid uplift (M30 → M42) | Critical/High CVE remediation only, Sev-1 workarounds, best-effort response | Bug fixes, compatibility, standard SLAs |
| **Custom Support Agreement** — bespoke, per-account (M42 → M54 max) | Negotiated scope, capped, priced at 2.5–3× original maintenance, minimum 12-month commitment, minimum contract value | Anything not explicitly enumerated |
| **End of Life** (M42 public / M54 absolute) | Nothing. Hosted instances decommissioned; on-prem software may run at customer's own risk with signed liability acknowledgment | — |

### 3.2 The calendar

| Milestone | Timing | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Confidential briefings, top 40 + OEMs** | M−1 | 3–4 weeks ahead of public, under NDA, exec-to-exec |
| **Public announcement** — full calendar, parity commitments, incentives, tooling roadmap | **M0** | Single coordinated moment: customers, partners, analysts, field, press |
| **End of Sale** — no new L customers | M0 | Immediate |
| **End of Expansion** — no new seats/capacity/modules on L | M12 | Grandfather in-flight projects case-by-case to M18 |
| **Feature freeze** (except adjudicated migration blockers) | M0 | Blocker exception process is the trust mechanism |
| **Parity Wave 1 GA** on Platform N | M9 | Highest-value rebuilt capabilities |
| **Migration tooling GA** (assessment + converter + parallel-run) | M9 | Must precede any pressure campaign |
| **Parity Wave 2 GA** | M15 | Completes committed rebuild scope |
| **Full Support ends → Maintenance Support** | M18 | |
| **Scale migration window** | M12–M30 | ~65% of accounts should cut over here |
| **Standard support ends** | **M30** | Extended Security Support begins, priced at 1.5× (M30–36), 2.0× (M36–42) |
| **Extended support ends; hosted decommission begins** | **M42** | |
| **Absolute EOL / hard stop** | **M54** | Custom Support Agreements only; nothing beyond |

**Runway rationale:** 30 months of standard support gives even a heavily customized enterprise two budget cycles and two change-freeze-free windows. 42 months total is defensible to auditors and regulators. Beyond that, escalating price does the persuading rather than escalating threats.

### 3.3 The security tripwire (state this up front, at M0)

Publish a named exception: *if an unpatchable Critical vulnerability appears in an out-of-support dependency, we will accelerate specific end-dates with 90 days' notice.* Saying this on day one converts a future betrayal into a pre-agreed, jointly understood condition — and it gives your CISO a legitimate lever instead of a fight.

---

## 4. Feature triage: rebuild vs. bridge vs. retire

### 4.1 Decision framework

Score every candidate capability (0–5 each):

- **A. Revenue dependency** — ARR of accounts that would be blocked without it
- **B. Obligation** — regulatory, contractual, or audit requirement (binary multiplier: if yes, rebuild)
- **C. Substitutability** — is there an acceptable workaround, partner product, API, or services path?
- **D. Strategic fit** — does it belong in N's architecture, or would it import legacy debt?
- **E. Rebuild cost** — engineering months, ongoing maintenance drag

| Outcome | Trigger | Commitment level |
|---|---|---|
| **Rebuild native** | High A, or B=yes; fits D | Named in public parity roadmap with a GA quarter and contractual remedy if missed |
| **Bridge** (compat shim, adapter, transpiler, plugin, partner) | High A, poor D — needed, but shouldn't live in the core | Shipped with *its own* sunset date (typically EOL+24m) |
| **Substitute** (services, one-time custom build, config recipe) | Moderate A, high C, low D | Funded by vendor for Tier 1/2; documented recipe for Tier 3 |
| **Retire** | Low A, high C | Named publicly with the replacement path and an appeal window |

| Archetype | Typical call | Why |
|---|---|---|

| Permission/workflow model quirks, granular admin semantics | **Rebuild the semantics**, not the UI | Cheap relative to the trust it buys; blocks admin sign-off otherwise |
| Long-tail flags, deprecated report variants, sub-1% toggles | **Retire** | This is where you fund the rest |

### 4.4 The Migration Blocker Board — your single most important trust mechanism

- **Any customer, any tier, can file a "Migration Blocker."** Public intake form, no gatekeeping by account size.
- **15-business-day adjudication SLA.** Four verdicts: *Rebuild (with quarter)*, *Bridge*, *Workaround (documented, validated with the customer)*, *Won't fix (with reasoning)*.
- **Public register** — all filings, status, verdicts, dates. Visible to all customers.
- **Cross-functional board**: Product (chair), Eng, CS, Sales, and a rotating customer advisory seat.
- **Reserved capacity:** hold 20–25% of the parity engineering budget unallocated for blockers discovered after M0. They *will* arrive, and refusing them is what breaks the program's credibility.

The register converts "you're abandoning us" into "there is a visible, fair process, and my issue is #47 with a Q3 date." That shift is worth more than any discount.

---

## 5. Migration tooling (the product you must actually build)

Treat this as a funded product with a PM, a roadmap, and its own SLAs. Under-tooling is the single most common cause of EOL programs slipping.

| Component | Purpose | Target |

| 10 | Financial model & investor narrative | Profit bridge, guidance treatment (§6) | CFO + IR |

### 3.1 Cover narrative and leak plan

Six months of instrumentation, funded audits, and contract review across 4,000 accounts and a field organization **will leak.** Plan for it rather than pretending otherwise.

- **Honest public framing from M−6:** *"We are running a Platform Modernization Assessment across our product line to plan the next decade of investment."* This is true, non-deniable-later, and consistent with the eventual announcement.
- **Leak-response kit ready at M−6:** pre-drafted holding statement, field FAQ, and an accelerated Tier 1 briefing sequence that can be triggered within 48 hours. If a credible leak occurs, we **pull the announcement forward** rather than deny it. Denial is the one action that cannot be recovered from.
- **Field discipline:** no rep is briefed on the EOL decision before M−1. Reps are given a truthful, sufficient answer for the assessment framing. Anyone who speculates on dates is corrected in writing.
- **Gate G0 exit criteria (see §11.2)** include "leak-response kit tested" and "Tier 1 briefing calendar locked."
